question.problem: The acceleration of a cyclist is $1.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ What is the cyclist's acceleration in ${\text{km/s}}^{2}?$
question.worked_solution:
We are given the units $\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}},$ and we want to convert this into $\frac{\text{km}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.$ To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us:

$$
\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}=\frac{\text{km}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}
$$

We want to replace $\text{m}$ with $\text{km}.$ To get rid of $\text{m},$ we can put $\text{m}$ in the denominator so that it cancels out. To introduce $\text{km},$ we can put $\text{km}$ in the numerator.

$$
\frac{\cancel{\text{m}}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{km}}{\cancel{\text{m}}}=\frac{\text{km}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}
$$

So, our conversion formula is

$$
\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{km}}{\text{m}}=\frac{\text{km}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The acceleration given in the problem statement is $1.5\,\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.$

- There are $1\,000$ meters per kilometer. Taking the reciprocal, there are $\frac{1}{1\,000}$ kilometers per meter.

Applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}1.5\,\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}} & =1.5\,\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{1\,000}\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{m}} \\  & =1.5\cdot \frac{1}{1\,000}(\frac{\cancel{\text{m}}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{km}}{\cancel{\text{m}}}) \\  & =0.001\,5\,\frac{\text{km}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the acceleration of the cyclist is $0.001\,5\,\text{km}/{\text{s}}^{2}.$
